sentences.text: Hi, Leslie.
Good afternoon.
Nice to see you again.
Yeah, good to see you again and nice to meet you, Leslie.
Nice to meet you, Andy.
Yeah, I was looking forward to hearing your accent as well.
How's things going in America?
Well, I get accused of having a bit of a mid Atlantic draw, but I can absolutely turn it on if I need to, but I don't need to communicate with, with waiters, so there you go.
Brilliant.
Brilliant.
You're in London, right?
Yeah, I am, yeah.
Well, actually I live in Somerset, so an office in London and we're based in New York and San Francisco.
A little bit of LA sometimes.
I spent six months in LA last year with the family.
So I'm definitely missing the weather.
It's raining a hell of a lot here.
Yeah, it was, it was beautiful.
It was in the.
About 70 degrees because I've learned to do Fahrenheit now and sunny at the weekend, so I don't miss the British winters.
Although I don't enjoy hurricane season here in the southeast, so.
No, it's a little bit scary, isn't it?
My sister in law lives in South Carolina as well, so.
Yeah.
Yeah.
So yeah, it's lovely down there.
It is.
Well, look, and you and I had a good call a couple of weeks ago and appreciate you spending a bit more time with us.
I think it might be good.
I mean, you've heard the, the sort of sanitized version of Leslie and her agency for me, but it might be good to, to get five or 10 minutes from.
I don't want to.
Sorry, I don't want to say from the horse's mouth, but you know, from, from Leslie herself.
And then it would also be good if you could just talk a little bit about your firm and what you guys do and how we might work together in timelines and all that kind of stuff.
Is that a good way to kick off here?
Yeah, sure.
That's exactly what I'd expect.
Yeah, that'd be great.
So obviously, Leslie, we've covered a lot already with Carl last week and I guess not really that.
That.
Well, I mean it is, but we've already got the information, you know, about the business itself.
So I guess really it's more about what your plans and goals are.
Okay.
And.
Yeah.
How you see a transaction happening.
Okay.
Although I try not to look or act it.
I am 58, so I, I don't want to get to the point that I just want to be done and retire.
But I also am thinking of slowing down and also, you know, the legacy I Mean, in.
In a very brief summary.
I know you have my background, but I set up HSD Communications in 1998 and I worked my way up through.
I mean, I started with the SART Group graduate trainee and they didn't have PR degrees back then in England, so I did.
I read history at uni and worked up and then decided to give it a go in 1998.
Set that up with nothing but, you know, one of those huge, huge desktop computers and a very big cell phone or mobile, and built it from there.
Enjoyed it enormously, worked 80 hours a week.
It's amazing what you can do if you work 80 hours a week and forget to have children.
But anyway, so I then exited in 2007, or we sold, which was obviously a great year to sell.
Gyro is now part of Dendhu, so HSD Communications is a tiny part of that.
We obviously, the recession wasn't great, 2008.
Nobody made their numbers in 2008, but I did my year, I did my handover.
We had the opportunity to come here.
I didn't.
Carl's originally American, as you probably figured.
This was a new part of the world.
There was some family and appeals to coming here.
So I enjoyed both weeks of my retirement in 2009.
Bit of a serial entrepreneur and a workaholic.
And I'll be honest with you, at first I thought, I'm not going to do employing people again.
You know, I mean, it was a lot.
It was a lot of work for many years and I'm proud of it.
But 2008 was fairly, you know, difficult for anybody in marketing and I thought, well, I'll just start doing some freelancing, giving back, serving on boards, because it was very humbling.
Nobody knew who Leslie Francis was, although I was Leslie Scott professionally.
I thought, might as well change my name, not just for Uncle Sam's bureaucracy and the tradition, but because, you know, didn't.
I didn't have a American presence.
Whereas Leslie Scott meant something back in the day in the uk, certainly in healthcare communications.
So really it was organic growth opportunity here.
I've been quite a sweet spot.
I don't know if you're aware of the southeast growth, but it is a growing area now.
It's a very different market to London, it's much smaller.
The budgets aren't the same, but of course the cost of living isn't the same either, and salaries aren't the same.
And we've built up through just hard work and largely word of mouth and of course had to evolve.
So although called the company Leslie Francis Public relations I thought, you know, I'll just have a couple of employees, I'll just stick with pr.
Everything's evolved, everything's changed.
We've had to go digital.
We offer graphic design, website development, social media and digital marketing is obviously a key part of what we do.
When I need to outsource Google advertising, that sort of thing I have.
We have a couple of partners we work with, so we really position ourselves as a full service agency.
Oh, and you do the old fashioned print broadcast media as well?
Of course.
Oh, we still do pr, of course.
I mean I say the PR and the public relations, many of the skills are the same.
The tools have just changed.
You know, it's not buying the old fashioned newspaper anymore, it's reading online.
So we have built up.
I have a group of younger women, I have one man, the website developer.
But marketing is very female dominated and women are very good at multitasking.
So we have a core group and we do well.
We have three core sectors.
I started in the nonprofit area serving and then beginning to work.
I'm kind of reducing that a little bit because it's not as profitable.
We do give 20% of our billable time to nonprofits and that's been a good marketing aspect for lfpr.
We sort of rebranded as LFPR Marketing to try and emphasize and communicate the diversity of the services we provide.
And that was about two years ago.
We have a significant sector in education and government and that's great money to have.
It's grant driven once you're on the budget line.
So we work for the city of Port went.
We actually created the whole marketing department for, for Bryan county from 2016 to 2020 and now that's the fastest growing county in Georgia.
And they took it in house because it got so big.
Sort of a victim of your own success.
But we still do projects for them and have a great relationship.
We work for charter school, we work for Georgia Tech and then we increasingly work for small and medium sized businesses.
We offer exclusivity in a lane.
So I wouldn't work for two realtors or two spas or whatever.
We give, you know, we give exclusivity there really the not not.
It's hard to find somebody who is as, you know, driven or whatever as I am.
And it's a next gen, it's a generation gal.
I have a great bunch of young women but you know, the, the eldest is early 30s and there's quite a gap in terms of Experience and age.
You know, I've also got the opportunity here that people see my global experience and I started in the trenches volunteering back here.
It was actually humbling but it was good for me and I do have a good, we do have a good reputation.
So I want to think very carefully about an exit and a transition.
Carl is clearly older than myself and he's semi retarded though he's an enormous help with the finances and the business as we have grown and he has other chairmanships and so on.
So he's certainly not, you know, an inactive retiree.
I'm not a trophy husband clearly.
So.
And I'm not a trophy wife anyway.
But you know, one does start to think about the next stage as one gets towards, you know, the.
Yes, the big six and beyond.
So it's really just thinking about I would love to have found somebody who could just be me.
Sounds really, you know, egotistical, but I haven't.
I have some good people that they're younger, they're less experienced, you know, they're having families and that's wonderful.

But although I joke, you know, you do need to be pretty focused and driven to, to run an agency and a lot of the people who are coming to the area this, I don't know if you know this old savannah and you have a few people and they all work between themselves and it's old fashioned PR and going to partisan.
That's lovely.
But that pond is expanded so much and a lot of people like the global experience I bring plus the many years here having that experience.
But also having seen Savannah grow and greater Savannah grow and that does, you know, we are getting approached a lot for new business.
We're small, I mean we're very small agency and a lot of that is because of the resource.
I won't understaff and over promise because I built my reputation up twice and I'm not going to throw that out of the window.
And also as I said, it's just a small market so it's really exploring how can I.
And I'm not in a hurry to do it in that I'm not going to say here you are, it's not like you know, selling a car, here's the deed and off you go.
You know, a lot of what we do as you know from your because it's your field is relationships and services.
So I would see any transition as being slow, not necessarily in terms of a deal but in terms of me going, you know, buy them off to Acapulco or wherever.
So I do think that it's very important to me, the, the fit.
I do see it as important to have job security and loyalty to my team.
But, you know, they're young, they move, they get married, they have kids and you know, they live their lives.
The whole gyro experience, you know, it worked out very well for us, but they sold to a different agency and of course 2008 was rough, so it wasn't the now I would have liked or expected.
And I intend to, we intend to stay in this region.
So I'd like some sort of.
It doesn't necessarily have to have my name on the door, but I would like to still be around and you know that, to just have the pride in it evolving into something.
So I don't know if that's too much information or helpful, but I'll shut up now.
No, as much information as possible.
So.
Good.
I think really it's just about what would look like a success for you, Leslie, in terms of an exit.
Having done a really successful exit, I'm pretty sure that you wouldn't be able to follow.
Follow it up anywhere near as closely in a sort of, you know, satisfying way in terms of like multiples and how that's going to set you up for the rest of your life.
So, you know, what, what is it that you're.
You're looking for outside of just, you know, a successor and being able to leave a legacy, you know, financially?
What, what would that look like?
What kind of multiple?
Carl, I'm going to let you take that one as my.
I mean, it's, it, it is financial, but it is, it is a bit more than financial as well because, you know, we are tied to this area and Leslie has reputation in terms of the whole.
She is the PR queen of the Southeast, Southeastern Georgia and doesn't want to, doesn't want to hand that over to somebody that's going to screw it up.
That being said, the likely buyer pool is agencies from Charlotte, Atlanta, Jacksonville, Tallahassee.
There's some big agencies there and they do nothing, literally nothing in the Southeast.
And so this would likely be an add on to that.
We all know that it's going to come with an earn out.
I mean, if someone's gonna, if someone's gonna buy it, they're gonna want the current clients to stay and some of the momentum to be maintained.
And so that means, you know, Leslie's gonna be around for two or three years.
And so I think that in, in terms of the shape of the deal we're comfortable with an earn out.
We know it's what we're selling is very earnoutable and so there's, there's that sort of lifestyle side of it.
The business will turn over 8 or 900,000 this year dollars.
And so next year is likely to be the million dollar plus year which is the biggest in the, in this part of the world.
But it's certainly not big in global terms.
Global terms, yeah.

So you know, I guess we would sort of having, having grown up in, in London 20 years ago with her other agency, we'd be thinking in terms of your traditional metrics, you know, three times billing billable fees or you know, some, some big multiple of adjusted ebit, you know.
So I guess it, I'm not really answering your question directly but you know.
Let me, let me try and answer it for you then.
Good to set your expectations.
So you did say that you had about a 30% profit margin.
So we're roughly a million, let's just use easy maths at 300k.
So most agencies, you know, doing revenue less than one, one and a half million, you can kind of expect pretty low multiple EBITDA.
So yes, it can be adjusted, that's for certain.
Obviously it's a lifestyle business and you'll be having some personal expenses or some one off stuff go through there that wouldn't go through next year.
So it's adjusted EBITDA and then it's a three to five times multiple.
So it's fairly low, I would say the sort of middle mark for agencies.
I know you'll have experienced probably a big multiple Leslie, because you got bought out by a big holding company.
But it was different time.
Yeah, it was, it was a boom time and it was right, it was right at the peak of the market before it completely collapsed.
Yeah, I was lucky.
I was lucky, very lucky.
But most sort of mid, you know, middle of the road agencies are going at a five, five and a half times multiple.

So even the holding companies are buying at the low end of the market and by that I mean sort of agencies that are doing so between 1 and 5 million EBITDA, they will buy those agencies for about 5, 5 and a half.
That's what they're shooting for.
The reality is if there's some kind of niche or high quality thing in there, then they will pay extra and they'll probably pay up to about 10, 11, 12 times multiples.
But the top end of the market is probably like a 12, 12 times multiple.
And I don't think that, you know, we'll be able to command that.
We're probably looking somewhere above the minimum multiple, around a four, maybe a five, depending on the sort of build up we can create in the selling process.
And really what we need to do is create some kind of contention where we've got one or two bidders at the table bidding against each other and really trying to leverage one against the other.
They really want to buy.
LESLIE FRANCIS PR because everybody's heard of it.
And like you say, they want to get into the Southeast.
And it's pretty, it's a pretty empty space, but high volume, high growth, etc.
Etc.
So, so, so just.
ANDY so those multiples you're talking about are on adjusted ebitda, right?
You're not, you're not talking multiples of revenue.
You're talking adjusted EBITDA.
Multiples of revenue.
It just doesn't happen in marketing services.
It doesn't happen mostly around service businesses, full stop.
But, you know, agencies is a pretty, it's a pretty sort of commoditized market in that, you know, there's a lot of players in the market already.
There's certainly, there's a lot of financial players that have come in over the last five to ten years.
But, but we are, you know, kind of in a buyer's market, I would say, you know, I don't, I mean.
I don't think, I don't think what you're saying in our expectations are a million miles from each other because, you know what?
So if we wind up with, you know, 3 or 3 or 350 adjusted EBITDA and you know, you put a high side multiple of 10 or 12 on that.
I mean, okay, you know, you're looking at sort of, again, just throwing wild numbers around.
You know, you're looking at circa 3 million bucks.
Yeah, that's probably pretty close to what, what our expectations are.
I mean, anybody selling something always believes that it's worth more, of course.
Yeah, double, at least.
So I would say, really, your expectation should be half of that.
So a 10x multiple is obviously the fantasy, but it's not very common in this area of the market.
I would say more likely a sort of conservative view would be a four or five times ebitda, and that's adjusted ebitda.
So obviously we want to do our best with that number because it's very significant to get a multiple, but it's more likely to be four to five times X.
And then the way that we can leverage that, like I say, is to get contention around the, the actual, during the actual process.
And that's, and that's really what, what our strong point is, Leslie, and this is what we discussed last time.
So what we're trying to do a.
Bit about your process and also how you target and also I don't want like to have a for sale sign outside.
We never do that.
It's always completely anonymous.
So what we're trying to do is create a six month process.
So the first month is really just setting up and doing the basics and then we're going out to market.
It's about two or three months of meeting and greeting.

We're trying to get as many meetings as we can and then we put a time limit on offers and that usually comes in around the fourth month, which gives us one or two months of due diligence and then contract negotiation.
And realistically that's usually somewhere between 30 and 60 days.
With a smaller business you can probably get all of that done within 30 days.
So it's, it's a, it's pretty much, I mean it's to the day there's a couple of deals we've done where it's been the day before, the day after a six month anniversary of us.
So it's a pretty tight process that we run.

But ideally around the third or fourth month we want one offer on the table and then we go back to all the other interested parties and say we have an offer on the table, we're looking for another one.
Because it's quite often more than more, more often than not that the offers that come in slightly later actually steal the deal.
So most, most serious buyers kind of, kind of know that.
Well, that happened in London actually.
Yeah, well, yeah.
So the way that we market that is we, we have a sort of a couple of different layers.
It's like spear, spear fishing and deep trawler fishing.
And then my, myself and David Tsutsumi, who's our managing director, who's based in San Francisco, we have a good personal network as well.
So we're, we're, we're going out doing research.
We have re researchers who will research the market for every single client that comes on board.
And they will be doing, I guess what the, what Carl was suggesting in that we will go out to all the local agencies in the Southeast.
We're going to be talking to everybody that's already around doing pr, doing digital marketing.
And we will be marketing directly to those guys.
And then we also have a database of 130,000 marketing agencies and agency Buyers and again, we can do a keyword search against those people that are already offering the same services.
So these won't be local buyers.
More likely they will be across the U.S.
for instance, we sold a company in LA to somebody in Chicago, sorry in New York and we sold somebody in Austin, Texas to somebody in Chicago.
So it's not always local, but they will match on services and they just want to expand.
Right.
So there'll be those types of buyers too.
And then we have a database of 20,000 subscribers as well.
We have agencies co platforms, which is a marketplace for agency owners to buy and sell their agencies.
It's free to list on there as well.

But we can, I mean we can normally tell within the first 24 hours if we've got a sort of hot listing because we'll get a lot of responses just from our own mailing list before we actually go out and do any, any other marketing.
What can I, can I ask, sorry, a couple of questions.

What, what length of earn out and in your experience, and also just initially from what you do know about lfpr, what type of, I mean we sit as somebody that would want a, it would be a strategic investment either because of the region or the specialty.
But I also want to ask a little bit about that sort of succession planning and having expertise from the, you know, the agency that potentially buys us.
It would really be helpful if you could talk to that for a moment or two.
Right.
So in terms of the likely buy you mean and what the process is with them.
Yes.
And also how long an earn out is usual, who you think, you know, the type of agent, the type of agency or purchase that you think would be most likely.
Yeah, the last time we sold an agency was about 15 years ago.
So give, give us the modern, give us the up to date view of big agency earn out thinking on buying little agencies and stuff like that.
We had this huge printed book.
I'm sure things have moved on.
Well actually the agency's market is very established, so things haven't really, I mean they were all established by Saatchi and Saatchi actually in the early days.
Martin Sorrel, he kind of, he established the rules for acquisition and they've been pretty much copied ever since.
Although he's groundbreaking again and doing a single balance sheet approach to what he's doing at the moment, most agencies haven't really moved on.
They're still doing the same kind of thing.
However, what I would say is every deal is different, every buyer is different, every seller's needs are different.
So what usually ends up happening is somewhere in the middle of what everybody is prepared to capitulate to the other side.
So for instance, you know, you can actually come to the market and say, I want to retire, I want to be out of this business as soon as possible.

We sold a business fairly recently and it wasn't a retirement sale or anything like that, but they, they were probably in the late 40s, early 50s and they had a second business that they were working on, a SaaS platform and so they wanted to get out within 12 months.
They actually hit all of their earn out targets within nine months and completely left the business in nine months.
But we went to market knowing that that's the outcome that they wanted.
Actually one of the things about you wanting to stay in the business longer potentially is that we would probably be able to get a much better price.

So if we, if you were to do a five year earn out, for instance, which is something we just did for a client that's based in Israel, we sold to a listed company in the US they have a 5 year earn out and because of that, that their earn out, their actual valuation is enormous.
I mean it was a huge, it was double what they asked us to get for them.
And because the founder is willing to stick around, there is a huge earn out attached to the back end.
So it's up to you really Lesley, if you want to get out quickly, the multiples will be not necessarily significantly lower, but they will certainly be a little bit lower.

So for instance, we could probably achieve like a 4x multiple on a 12 month earn out and we'll probably get for a 3 year earn out like a 5x multiple and then a 5 year round out we may well get 6 or 7 times.
I'm just setting expectations here.
It might be that we go through your, your books and you know, your decks and, and it could, we could, you know, end up getting one ones or twos above those.
Kind of.
Good to know.
And I didn't want to wait till I was just exhausted and done quite specifically.

Well, again, you know, considering, you know, what you said at the start, I, in terms of leaving a legacy and that sort of thing and maintaining the brand, those things kind of go hand to hand with a long earn out.

So you know, somebody that was buying it, particularly in the set from the Southeast, one of the states based in the Southeast that was looking to expand, they would want the Leslie Francis PR brand to probably stay there for as long as possible.

So you sticking with the business and Being the face of the business, even if you weren't heavily involved in the day to day, but just as an ambassador for the business or chairwoman for the business, then there would be a better multiple.
Whether it would be significantly better, I don't know.
I would say probably an extra 1 or 2 for the amount but obviously that's significant on top of a salary and all the other perks that you could expect to be an employee of a larger organization.
So lots of travel.

We actually sold this fairly small business, definitely sub 1 million based in Los Angeles to a New York company and at the start of this year and the founder is now doing lots of traveling across the States which he absolutely.
But was also able to take a full four week holiday which he's never done before before in his life.
What's a holiday?
Exactly.
But he now has other people to worry about trying to find everybody's salaries.
So you know, it's a completely different lifestyle but obviously it's a much more secure lifestyle for the seller as well.
So.
Absolutely.
I mean I remember with Jara, you know, I was off to Dubai, I was, you know, all over the UK and Europe.
So I, I remember that year and you know, especially before things went south with the economy generally, so which wasn't long after.
It wasn't long after, but the first few months.
So up until about the June was doing a lot of that.
So really we can just go to market with whatever your ideal is and we will dig into this.

Once we, we've signed an engagement letter, we have a kickoff call with my deal team who will go through lots and lots of questions with you to try and get a really good understanding of what it is that you want to achieve, but also get an understanding of the business as well so that they can sell it to people that are interested.
But we will go to market with whatever the ideal scenario is.
And then what tends to happen even with people that want to get out quickly is we sometimes have really exciting buyers come in.
They're a big organization, they want the founder to stay in as long as possible and everything changes at the deal table anyway.
So.
But, but you know, the idea is really to go in, to be as flexible as possible and just to refer against something you asked earlier about what types of buyers is.
We just don't, we don't take anything off the table at the start.
You know, we, we want to go out to the, to everybody in the market and get under as many noses as possible and then let's just see what happens.
It may be that later on we decide to just focus in one area because you've not enjoyed having conversation with big corporates, for instance.
And so we just stick with single buyers.
Cultural, cultural fit is going to be important for me, especially if I have a long earn out.
Yeah, of course, of course.
But also there is one other type of buyer that I think we'll see at this end of the market and that's the SBA buyer.
So these tend to be owner operators.
They are looking to move into the area, for instance, and maybe they've worked in a big agency in New York and they want to move to Savannah or to the area they can get a loan secured against.

The SBA lenders, usually up to about 5 million for an acquisition and they just want to buy the business, keep you in for as long as they need to get the handover from your current clients and then they're happy to take the business and run with it.
And those multiples usually tend to be around the 4, 3 to 5x multiple.
The SBA lenders are fairly conservative.
But the fact that you've been around for a long time, you've got a great track record will stand you in good stead for the higher end of those numbers.
Thank you.
Can I ask a couple of questions, Andy, on the Agencies co website, which is very good by the way.
I mean you, you basically advertise an asking price.
I mean I, so I guess in, in my old fashioned way of thinking you throw, you know, you put the business up and then you take offers.
But I mean, you actually say this is the asking price.
I mean, how, how.
And it's pretty, I mean it's hard to see a lot of rhyme or reason between some of the turnovers, some of the asking prices.
So I know it depends on different, you know, sectors and opportunities and everything.
But how, how successful are you at achieving those asking prices?
Yeah, so we are usually relatively conservative when we go into those conversations.
We want to have a believable price, but also we want to set expectations for the buyers as well.

We have very ambitious sellers that we work with not only for themselves but for their teams and they want, you know, they want to get the best price for sometimes, you know, once in a lifetime opportunity to sell.
So, so sometimes they are on the high end and I think buyers, because we work on the buy side a lot as well, I think buyers will take those as an indication.
But if they are super serious buyers, it isn't a deal that's going to always end up about the price, it's about lots of other things and they know that.
So even if we price something that's stupidly high, if we have a serious buyer who's very experienced, they will understand what the metrics are for a seller.
Right.
And, and if they financially come in, let's just say, you know, we market something at 10x.
If they come in at a 4 or 5 times multiple because they, they understand the market better, they will know that the seller will need something else.
You know, whether that's a long earn out trying to achieve some more of that expectation or whether it's other factors.
You know, it might just be that they only want to work 10 hours a week or you know, et cetera, et cetera.
It could be other things.
But they know they've got sweeten the deal based on whatever the price is even if they can't get there just financially.
So, but we tend to achieve, and this is because we, we really want to be part of the process where we value the business as well.
But obviously there's costs attached to that and there's different pricing, but we tend to achieve much better actual valuations for the, for the deal than what we market.
So it's not a case of us going to the market too cheap and then everybody knocking us down from that.
Actually mostly I would say the buyers are very, they're very sophisticated and they understand what a deal's got to look like for both sides to make sense.
And quite often if they're, they're funded, you know, from a debt lender, they need to go with a good story to those guys.
They want to get excited by the price and lots of other things.
So coming in too cheap will actually put off the lenders as well.
So, so actually, you know, if they've got really good sort of lenders that come from a more acquisitive market, those lenders want to get excited by the story.

So you know, paying a 10x for a very established business with a named leader that wants to stay in the business for five years, that may command a better multiple than we've actually listed for as well.
So, so yeah, so it's not just bargain basement shopping and trying to sell it for as cheap as possible.
Okay, I have two other quick questions.
I think I know the answer to this one.
So we have a, a building as well.
Now the building is in the, is in the, is titled in a different entity.
Presumably most agencies, they don't want real estate.
They're not interested.
No.
Right, okay.
Rentable.
So that's not an issue, that's an investment property.
Or just rent it to yourself and sign yourself up for a five year contract.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
All right.
And, and so just to stick that in a pension fund or something else, the property, and just rent it back to the business.
Yeah, yeah.
Okay.
And second question.
So we're entering into the silly season now.
You know, everybody next week.
Yeah, everybody's got diary congestion.
Thanksgiving, Christmas parties, you know, breaks at Christmas.
Everyone wants to take a breath after the elections here.
I mean there's a lot, there's.
Things will slow down pretty dramatically over the next six weeks.
So at what point, again, keeping in mind that we're not in a big hurry, but we also know we need to get on with it.
